**Payload Electronics — Component Research**

_Sensor picks, system diagram, MCU choice, storage plan, risks, and fall next steps_

# Sensors

## Pressure & temperature

Same chip measures both.

| **Spec**              | **MS5611**                   | **BMP390**                |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| **Accuracy**          | ±1.5 mbar (≈ 10 cm altitude) | ±3 Pa (≈ 0.25 m altitude) |
| **Speed**             | 100+ Hz                      | up to ≈200 Hz             |
| **Interface & power** | I2C/SPI, <1.4 mA             | I2C/SPI, <650 µA          |
| **Cost**              | ≈ \$10                       | ≈ \$10                    |

Pick: MS5611 — the standard altimeter chip in student rocketry. BMP390 is the backup.

## Vibration

Measures shock and vibration through flight, including ignition and parachute deployment.

| **Spec**              | **ADXL375**      | **ICM-42688-P**       |
| --------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------- |
| **Range**             | ±200 g           | ±16 g max             |
| **Bandwidth**         | ≈ 1 kHz          | up to ≈1.6 kHz+       |
| **Interface & power** | I2C/SPI, ≈145 µA | I2C/SPI/I3C, ≈0.88 mA |
| **Cost**              | ≈ \$15           | ≈ \$15–\$35           |

Pick: ADXL375 — ±200 g range, won't clip on shock. ICM-42688-P adds spin/attitude data if the team wants it later, but its ±16 g range risks clipping.

## Humidity

Adds relative humidity to the pressure/temperature reading.

| **Spec**              | **SHT40**                   | **BME280**                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| **Accuracy**          | ±1.8% RH, ±0.2 °C           | ±3% RH, ±1 hPa pressure             |
| **Also measures**     | Humidity & temperature only | Humidity, temperature, and pressure |
| **Interface & power** | I2C, low power              | I2C/SPI, low power                  |
| **Cost**              | ≈ \$6–\$8                   | ≈ \$8–\$10                          |

Pick: SHT40 — more accurate than BME280, and keeps MS5611 as the pressure sensor.

## GPS / position

Timestamps and geotags every reading. Wind speed and direction come from horizontal drift during the parachute descent.

| **Spec**              | **NEO-M9N**                          | **NEO-M8N**                      |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| **Accuracy**          | ≈ 1.5 m, 4 satellite systems at once | ≈ 2.5 m, up to 3 systems at once |
| **Update rate**       | up to 25 Hz                          | up to 10 Hz                      |
| **Interface & power** | I2C/UART, ≈31 mA tracking            | UART/I2C, similar draw           |
| **Cost**              | ≈ \$70 (full-featured breakout)      | ≈ \$20–\$30 (common breakout)    |

Pick: NEO-M8N — cheaper, and accurate enough for this. Consumer GPS chips cap around 4 g / 500 m/s, so expect a brief loss of lock during motor boost. Mount the antenna on fiberglass or plastic — carbon fiber blocks GPS signal.

# System Diagram

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Power flows from the regulator to both sensors and the microcontroller. Sensors report over I2C/SPI to the Teensy, which timestamps and logs each sample to the microSD card. USB handles programming; the avionics link is optional.

# Microcontroller: Teensy 4.1 vs. ESP32

| **Spec**    | **Teensy 4.1**                    | **ESP32**                              |
| ----------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| **Speed**   | 600 MHz, single core              | 240 MHz, dual core                     |
| **Memory**  | 1 MB RAM / 8 MB flash             | 520 KB RAM / 4 MB flash                |
| **SD card** | Built-in, fast slot               | Usually slower; shares pins with flash |
| **Radio**   | None — quieter near GPS/altimeter | Wi-Fi + Bluetooth always on board      |
| **Timing**  | Nothing competes for CPU time     | Background Wi-Fi tasks can add jitter  |
| **Price**   | ≈ \$31.50                         | ≈ \$10.00                              |

Pick: Teensy 4.1 — cleaner sampling loop, built-in SD slot, no radio nearby. ESP32 is the pick for wireless telemetry or a tight budget.

# Storage Plan

| **Channel**               | **Rate** | **Data per flight** |
| ------------------------- | -------- | ------------------- |
| **Pressure & temp**       | 100 Hz   | ≈ 0.6 MB            |
| **Vibration**             | 800 Hz   | ≈ 4.8 MB            |
| **Total (packed binary)** | —        | ≈ 5.4 MB            |

As plain-text CSV instead of packed binary: ≈ 30–45 MB per flight. An 8–32 GB microSD card covers a full season many times over. The Teensy timestamps every sample from one shared clock, so pressure and vibration data stay aligned.

# Major Risks

- Sensor clipping — not enough range cuts off shock data.
- Power sag at ignition — give the regulator margin to avoid a reset.
- Slow SD writes — buffer in RAM so a slow write doesn't drop a sample.
- Loose wiring — use locking connectors and strain relief.
- Shared-bus lockup — split sensors across separate I2C/SPI buses.
- Corrupted log file — flush/close the file periodically.
- Radio noise — keep sensor wiring short and away from trackers or altimeters.

# Fall Next Steps

1. Breadboard the MS5611 + ADXL375 on the Teensy 4.1 and confirm logging works at full speed.
2. Measure real power draw, size the battery and regulator, and test recovery from a brief power dip.
3. Shake-test the prototype (or fly it non-critically) to confirm mounting and sample rates actually capture what we need.
